title: The Three Ages of Boss Rule
author: Stephen Eide
summary: Guest essay by Stephen Eide (Manhattan Institute) in Aaron Renn's newsletter analyzes three films as a complete and rarely acknowledged arc of American machine politics. Scorsese's Gangs of New York shows the origin: ward heelers replace warlords, Tammany Hall manages the conflict between Irish immigrants and nativists, and the Union Army's suppression of the 1863 draft riots forces the Irish to become Americans -- machine politics as civilizing function. Sturges' The Great McGinty depicts bossism at its peak: the boss stays behind the scenes (only two of twenty surveyed bosses were mayors), machine politics is genuinely democratic (enabling rises from the soup line to the governorship), and lines between reformer and boss are porous. Ford's The Last Hurrah shows the decline: Frank Skeffington (based on James Michael Curley) loses to a packaged nebbish candidate because the lace-curtain Irish no longer need ethnic demagoguery. The bosses fell not primarily because Progressives won but because rising Irish prosperity made the immigrant coalition unnecessary. Eide's argument: derided as corrupt engines, the machines actually managed conflict, integrated immigrants, enabled talent to rise from below, and made cities function -- and their decline heralded 'a generation of ciphers' whose inauthenticity politics has never recovered from.
points: * The urban party machines excelled at managing conflict -- the essential governance function that technical-reform accounts of city government consistently underrate relative to service delivery. * Machine politics was genuinely democratic: it enabled men to rise from exceedingly humble beginnings to positions of high authority, with Harry Truman and Tom Pendergast as the exemplary real-life case. * The bosses fell not primarily because Progressives succeeded but because New Deal welfare programs devalued the machines' currency and rising prosperity produced a lace-curtain Irish constituency that no longer needed ethnic demagoguery. * Their decline ushered in 'a generation of ciphers' -- packaged, handled, and promoted candidates whose inauthenticity the machines never had; the backlash against scriptedness (Cain, Perot) reflects the hunger for the authentic political figure the machines produced. * Scorsese, Sturges, and Ford are the only directors who took city politics seriously as subject matter -- the triumph of Progressive municipal reform made politics less colorful, and serious filmmakers have largely looked past it ever since.
quotes: The urban party machines excelled at managing conflict.
Government is much more than just a fee-for-service arrangement.
Parties are as natural to democracy as churches to religion.
machine politics was genuinely democratic in the sense that it enabled men to rise from exceedingly humble beginnings to positions of high authority.
The phrase used in Hurrah the novel is 'a generation of ciphers.'
Politicians would thenceforth be packaged, handled and promoted like so many different brands of soap.
Gangs argues that boss rule was an improvement over what came before: the gangs were just as corrupt, more violent, less enlightened, and, most crucially, pettier.
